There are basically three kinds of science. Settled, tentative and speculative. Settled are things we know for certain. Theories that are rock solid or facts that have been verified over and over. Earth is round, Newton's laws are accurate, life evolves, relativity works, quantum weirdness is real, planet is warming, vaccines don't cause autism. Settled science is never overthrown, only expanded upon.

Tentative is when we have a fairly clear picture, but there's still room for doubt. Dark matter is here. We're fairly certain it's real, but can't quite figure out what it is. It'll move to settled within a decade or two, I think.

Speculative is exactly what it sounds like: speculation. String theory, multiverses, all that. It might turn out to be right, but there's really no evidence either way.

No, heisenberg uncertainty isn't caused by device limitations. It is a consequence of measurements being incompatible. It doesn't say that you can't know the location of an object with infinite precision. It does say that if you try to find out, the object's momentum becomes so uncertain you'll have to provide it with infinite energy.

The best example is a string of stern gerlach experiments. It's written well in Sakurai, but I'll summarize. You perform a SG measurement on a beam of particles. They diverge in spin up and spin down. Now the incompatibility of the spin in different directions tells you that each beam will give you a 50/50 split in spin left and spin right if you do a SG measurement on one of these with the detector rotated 90°. Now you can select the beam spin up -> spin left. But measuring spin left made spin up/down uncertain again. So measuring that will split the beam again.
